div.head: SUBSECT. 2.
Quantity of diet a cause.
div.p: There is not so much harm proceeding from the substance itself of meat, and quality of it, in ill dressing and preparing, as there is from the quantity, disorder of time and place, unseasonable use of it, Animae negotium illa facessit & de templo dei immundum stabulum facit [That produces trouble of the soul, and makes a filthy stable of the temple of God]. Pelecyus 10 cap.intemperance, overmuch, or over-little taking of it. A true saying it is, Plures crapula quam gladius, this gluttony kills more than the sword, this omnivorantia & homicida gula, this all-devouring and murdering gut. And that of Lib. 11 cap. 52.Pliny is truer, Simple Diet is the best, heaping up of several meats, is pernicious, and sauces worse, many dishes bring many diseases. 3. 1 doc. 2 cap. 7.Avicenna cries out, that nothing is worse than to feed on many dishes, or to protract the time of meats longer than ordinary; from thence proceed our infirmities, and ’tis the fountain of all diseases, which arise out of the repugnancy of gross humours. Thence, saith Path. lib. 1 cap. 14.Fernelius, come crudities, wind, oppilations, Cacochymia, Plethora, Cachexia, Bradiopepsia, Juv. Sat. 1.Hinc subitae mortes, atque intestata senectus [thence sudden deaths and intestate old age], sudden death, &c., and what not.

As a Lamp is choked with a multitude of Oil, or a little fire with overmuch wood quite extinguished; so is the natural heat with immoderate eating, strangled in the Body. Pernitiosa sentina est abdomen insaturabile: one saith, an insatiable paunch is a pernicious sink, & the fountain of all diseases, both of Body and Mind. Nimia repletio ciborum facit melancholicum [Excessive repletion with foodstuffs causes melancholy].Mercurialis will have it a peculiar cause of this private disease; Solenander, consil. 5 sect. 3, illustrates this of Mercurialis, with an example of one so melancholy, ab intempestivis commessationibus, unseasonable feasting. Comestio superflua cibi, & potus quantitas nimia [Unnecessary consumption of food and too large a quantity of drink].Crato confirms as much, in that often cited Counsel, 21 lib. 2, putting superfluous eating for a main cause. But what need I seek further for proofs? Hear Hippocrates himself, Lib. 2 Aphoris. 10, Impure bodies the more they are nourished, the more they are hurt, for the nourishment is putrefied with vicious humours.

And yet for all this harm, which apparently follows surfeiting and drunkenness, see how we luxuriate and rage in this kind, read what Johannes Stuckius hath written lately of this subject, in his great Volume De Antiquorum Conviviis, and of our present age; Quam Vid. Goclen. de portentosis coenis, &c. Puteani Com.portentosae coenae, [what] prodigious suppers, Amb. lib. de Jeju. cap. 14.qui dum invitant ad coenam, efferunt ad sepulchrum
[who, when they invite you to dinner, are carrying you to the grave], what Fagos, Epicures, Apiciuses, Heliogabaluses our times afford? Lucullus’ ghost walks still, and every man desires to sup in Apollo: Aesop’s costly dish is ordinarily served up.

lg.l: ——— Juvenal.Magis illa juvant, quae pluris emuntur.
[… The things which cost more give more pleasure.]

div.p:
The dearest Cates are best, and ’tis an ordinary thing to bestow twenty or thirty pound on a dish, some thousand Crowns upon a dinner: Guicciardine.Mully-Hamet, King of Fez and Morocco, spent three pound on the sauce of a Capon: it is nothing in our times, we scorn all that is cheap. We loathe the very light (some of us, as Nat. quaest. 4, cap. ult.Seneca notes) because it comes free, and we are offended with the Sun’s heat, and those cool blasts, because we buy them not. This air we breathe is so common, we care not for it; nothing pleaseth but what is dear. And if we be Ingeniosi ad Gulam [Gifted at gluttony].witty in anything, it is ad gulam [in appetite]: if we study at all, it is erudito luxu [in learned luxury], to please the palate, and to satisfy the gut. A Cook of old was a base knave (as Livy complains), but now a great man in request: Cookery is become an art, a noble science: Cooks are Gentlemen: Venter Deus [the belly is god]: they wear their brains in their bellies, and their guts in their heads; as Epist. 28 lib. 7.Agrippa taxed some parasites of his time, rushing on their own destruction, as if a man should run upon the point of a sword, usque dum rumpantur comedunt [they eat till they burst] In lucem coenat Sertorius [Sertorius feasts until daylight].all day, all night, let the Physician say what he will, imminent danger, and feral diseases are now ready to seize upon them, they will eat till they vomit, Edunt ut vomunt, vomunt ut edant [they eat to vomit, and vomit to eat], saith Seneca; which Dion relates of Vitellius, Solo transitu ciborum nutriri judicatus: his meat did pass through, and away; or till they burst again. Seneca.Strage animantium ventrem onerant [They fill their belly with the butchery of animals], and rake over all the world, as so many Mancipia gulae, dapes non sapore sed sumptu aestimantes [Slaves to gluttony, they rate banquets not by flavour but by expense]. Seneca consol. ad Helviam.slaves, belly-gods, and land-serpents, et totius orbis ventri nimis angustus [and all the earth’s too small for their belly], the whole world cannot satisfy their appetite. Aeneas Silvius de miser. curial.Sea, Land, Rivers, Lakes, &c., may not give content to their raging guts. To make up the mess, what immoderate drinking in every place? Senem potu pota trahebat anus [The drunken old woman dragged the drunken old man], how they flock to the Tavern: as if they were fruges consumere nati, born to no other end but to eat and drink, like Ofellius Bibulus, that famous Roman parasite, qui dum vixit, aut bibit aut minxit [who while he lived was either drinking or pissing]; as so many Casks to
hold wine, yea worse than a Cask, that mars wines, and itself is not marred by it, yet these are brave men, Silenus Ebrius [Silenus drunk] was no braver. Et quae fuerunt vitia, mores sunt [And what used to be vices are customs]: ’tis now the fashion of our times, an honour: Nunc vero res ista eo rediit (as Chrysost. serm. 30 in 5 Ephes. Comments), ut effeminatae ridendaeque ignaviae loco habeatur, nolle inebriari; ’tis now come to that pass, that he is no Gentleman, a very milksop, a clown, of no bringing up, that will not drink, fit for no company; he is your only gallant that plays it off finest, no disparagement now to stagger in the streets, reel, rave, &c., but much to his fame and renown; as in like case Epidicus told Thesprio his fellow servant, in the Plautus.Poet. Aedepol facinus improbum [By god, a vile deed], one urged, the other replied, At jam fecere idem, erit illi illa res honori [but others have done the same before; this affair will turn out to his honour], ’tis now no fault, there be so many brave examples to bear one out; ’tis a credit to have a strong brain, and carry his liquor well: the sole contention who can drink most, and fox his fellow soonest. ’Tis the summum bonum [highest good] of our Tradesmen, their felicity, life and soul, Tanta dulcedine affectant, saith Pliny, lib. 14 cap. 22, ut magna pars non aliud vitae praemium intelligat [so sweet are its attractions … that a great part of mankind thinks there’s no other reward in life], their chief comfort, to be merry together in an Alehouse or Tavern, as our modern Muscovites do in their Mead-Inns, and Turks in their Coffee-houses, which much resemble our Taverns; they will labour hard all day long to be drunk at night, and spend totius anni labores [the labours of a whole year], as St. Ambrose adds, in a tippling feast; convert day into night, as Seneca taxeth some in his times, Pervertunt officia noctis & lucis [they reverse the duties of night and day]; when we rise, they commonly go to bed, like our Antipodes,

l.hi: Nosque ubi primus equis oriens afflavit anhelis,

lg.l: Illis sera rubens accendit lumina vesper.
[And when the rising sun first breathes on us with panting horses,
There reddening Vesper lights his evening fire.]

div.p: So did Petronius in Tacitus, Heliogabalus in Lampridius,

lg.l: [… in the nights he would stay awake until
Dawn, and would snore the whole day …]

div.p:
Smindyrides the Sybarite, never saw the Sun rise or set, so much as once in twenty years. Verres, against whom Tully so much inveighs, in Winter he was never extra tectum [outdoors], vix extra lectum, never almost out of bed, Diei brevitas conviviis, noctis longitudo stupris conterebatur [The short span of the day was wasted with banquets, the length of the night with debauchery].still wenching, and drinking; so did he spend his time, and so do Myriads in our days. They have gymnasia bibonum [drinking colleges], schools and
rendezvous; these Centaurs and Lapithae, toss pots, and bowls, as so many balls, invent new tricks, as Sausages, Anchovies, Tobacco, Caviar, pickled Oysters, Herrings, Fumades, &c., innumerable salt meats to increase their appetite, and study how to hurt themselves by taking Antidotes, Et quo plus capiant, irritamenta excogitantur [And so that they may enjoy more, stimulants are contrived].to carry their drink the better: Ambros.and when naught else serves, they will go forth, or be conveyed out to empty their gorge, that they may return to drink afresh. They make laws, insanas leges, contra bibendi fallacias [crazy rules against cheating in drinking], and Ingentia vasa velut ad ostentationem, &c. [Enormous cups, as if for display, etc.]brag of it when they have done, crowning that man that is soonest gone, as their drunken predecessors have done, ——— Plautus.quid ego video? Ps: Cum corona Pseudolum ebrium tuum ——— [what do I see? Pseudolus: Your drunken Pseudolus, with a crown …] And when they are dead, will have a Can of Wine with Lib. 3 Anthol. cap. 20.Maron’s old woman to be engraven on their tombs. So they triumph in villainy, and justify their wickedness; with Rabelais that French Lucian, drunkenness is better for the body than Physic, because there be more old drunkards, than old Physicians. Many such frothy arguments they have, Gratiam conciliant potando [They procure friendship by drinking].inviting and encouraging others to do as they do, and love them dearly for it (no glue like to that of good fellowship). So did Alcibiades in Greece, Nero, Bonosus, Heliogabalus in Rome, or Alegabalus rather, as he was styled of old (as Notis ad Caesares [From the stamp impressions referring to the Caesars].Egnatius proves out of some old Coins). So do many great men still, as Lib. de educandis principum liberis.Heresbachius observes. When a Prince drinks till his eyes stare, like Bitias in the Poet,

and comes off clearly, sound Trumpets, Fife and Drums, the spectators will applaud him, the Bishop himself (if he belie them not) with his Chaplain will stand by and do as much, O dignum principe haustum [a draught worthy of a prince!], ’twas done like a Prince. Our Dutchmen invite all comers with a pail and a dish, Velut infundibula integras obbas exhauriunt, & in monstrosis poculis, ipsi monstrosi monstrosius epotant [like funnels they drain whole beakers, and in monstrous cups, monstrous themselves, they drink even more monstrously], making barrels of their bellies. Incredibile dictu [Incredible to say], as Bohemus in Saxonia. Adeo immoderate & immodeste ab ipsis bibitur, ut in compotationibus suis non cyathis solum & cantharis sat infundere possint, sed impletum mulctrale apponant, & scutella injecta hortantur quemlibet ad libitum potare [Their drinking is so excessive and shameless that, in their carousing, they not only pour out cups and tankards but serve up a full milking-pail, and invite anyone to put their bowl in to drink at their pleasure].one of their own Countrymen complains: Quantum
liquoris immodestissima gens capiat, &c., How they love a man that will be drunk, crown him and honour him for it, hate him that will not pledge him, stab him, kill him: a most intolerable offence, and not to be forgiven. Qui potare recusat, hostis habetur, & caede nonnumquam res expiatur [He who refuses to drink is held to be an enemy, and sometimes the matter is resolved with bloodshed].He is a mortal enemy that will not drink with him, as Munster relates of the Saxons. So in Poland, he is the best servitor, and the honestest fellow, saith Alexander Guagninus, that drinketh most healths to the honour of his master, he shall be rewarded as a good servant, and held the bravest fellow that carries his liquor best, when as a Brewer’s horse will bear much more than any sturdy drinker, yet for his noble exploits, in this kind, he shall be accounted a most valiant man, for Graec. Poeta apud Stobaeum, ser. 18.tam inter epulas fortis vir esse potest ac in bello, as much valour is to be found in feasting, as in fighting, and some of our City Captains, and Carpet-Knights will make this good, and prove it. Thus they many times wilfully pervert the good temperature of their bodies, stifle their wits, strangle nature, and degenerate into beasts.

Some again are in the other extreme, and draw this mischief on their heads by too ceremonious and strict diet, being over-precise, Cockney-like, and curious in their observation of meats, times, as that Medicina statica prescribes, just so many ounces at dinner, which Lessius enjoins, so much at supper, not a little more, nor a little less, of such meat, and at such hours, a diet drink in the morning, Cock-broth, China-broth, at dinner, Plum broth, a Chicken, a Rabbit, rib of a Rack of Mutton, wing of a Capon, the Merrythought of a Hen, &c., to sounder bodies this is too nice and most absurd. Others offend in overmuch fasting: Pining adays, saith Qui de die jejunant & nocte vigilant facile cadunt in melancholiam; & qui naturae modum excedunt [Those who fast in the day and stay awake in the night easily fall into melancholy; and so do those who exceed the due measure of nature], cap. 5. Tract. 15 cap. 2. Longa famis tolerantia, ut iis saepe accidit qui tanto cum fervore Deo servire cupiunt per jejunium, quod maniaci efficiantur; ipse vidi saepe [Long endurance of hunger, as frequently occurs with those who ardently desire to serve God through fasting, turns them into maniacs; I’ve often seen this myself].Guainerius, and waking anights, as many Moors and Turks in these our times do. Anchorites, Monks, and the rest of that superstitious rank (as the same Guainerius witnesseth, that he hath often seen to have happened in his time) through immoderate fasting, have been frequently mad. Of such men belike Hippocrates speaks, 1 Aphor. 5, when as he saith, They more offend in too sparing diet, and are worse damnified, than they that feed liberally, and are ready to surfeit.
